arambai: Burmese horsemen who throw darts and miss a lot, yet a stray dart still hits whatever it lands on. That turns their poor aim into a strength against packed armies: a big group firing into clumped infantry or archers wrecks it in seconds, while a handful of Arambai achieves little. They hit hard and die fast, so they work best in numbers with someone else holding the line.
arbalester: The Archer line at full strength and the late game ranged backbone for many civilizations. A big group fires volleys that shred anything unable to close the distance, Halberdiers and Heavy Camel Riders above all, and from behind a wall it can pick off attackers safely. Against cavalry it needs hit and run micro, and it does almost nothing to rams. Before the Definitive Edition the unit was called the Arbalest, which is the name of the heavy steel crossbow itself.
archer: Archers are the usual tool for an early rush. A group can shoot Villagers over quick walls and pick off infantry before it gets close, and since they cost no food the attacker keeps saving it for the next age, while the Scouts and Skirmishers needed to stop them eat into the defender's food. They are also the most fragile military unit in the game, and their value drops fast once Knights and Mangonels appear.
armored-elephant: South Asian civilizations break walls with this elephant in place of the Battering Ram, and the game counts it as cavalry with a big bonus against buildings. Monks heal it from a safe distance, so a push needs no Villagers on the front line, though it will wander off after enemy units if nobody watches it. Paying food instead of wood makes it awkward early and comfortable late. Ancient Indian armies really did this: trained elephants battered gates and were called "town-breakers".
ballista-elephant: A Scorpion strapped to an elephant, firing bolts that pass through every unit in a line. It counts as cavalry, so Monks heal it instead of Villagers repairing it, and it can garrison in a Castle. With far more hit points than a Scorpion and no minimum range, it needs much less babysitting. It can also shoot down trees one at a time, which opens paths through dense forest on maps like Black Forest.
battering-ram: Rams exist to knock down buildings, and in the Castle Age nothing does it better. Arrows barely scratch them, so a few rams in front of an army soak up archer fire, and a ram battering a Castle even shields the Villager repairing it from the Castle's arrows. Infantry garrisoned inside make it faster and hit buildings harder. Melee units tear it apart, though: with the lowest melee armor in the game, a ram loses a straight fight to a single Villager.
battle-elephant: Battle Elephants are slow, heavy cavalry shared by six South and Southeast Asian civilizations, each with its own bonus or technology for them. A single Stable turns out far more hit points in elephants than in Knights, so a player can switch into them fast to hold a push or surprise an opponent. They have been hard to balance: Khmer elephants were once so strong that the Elite attack and the trample damage were cut for everyone.
berserk: Viking axemen who heal themselves over time, so a group that survives one fight walks into the next one close to full strength. They are quick for infantry and can catch small groups of foot archers, though big archer masses still beat them. A Viking player usually picks either Berserks or the Champion line, since upgrading both rarely pays off. Berserks were the first unit in the game to regenerate, and their horned helmets are pure invention: Viking warriors never wore them in battle.
blackwood-archer: Tupi archers that come out of the Castle two at a time and take half a population slot each, so they are meant to be massed. Each one is fragile, with the lowest hit points of any regular unit, but a fast rate of fire lets them chip through armor that would stop other archers. The Curare technology adds poison that ignores armor and stacks across archers, and part of the cost comes back whenever one dies.
bolas-rider: A Mapuche mounted archer built for catching things. Its charged shot is a bolas that hits harder and slows the target, so Mapuche infantry and foot archers can run down units that would otherwise get away. A bonus against cavalry makes it a good answer to enemy horsemen, though it is frailer than a Cavalry Archer and needs numbers. The slow does not stack, so attack move or patrol works better than focus fire, letting each rider snare a different target.
bombard-cannon: The Bombard Cannon outranges every generic tower and Castle, so it can knock down defenses from a safe spot without the packing and unpacking a Trebuchet needs. Its shots are accurate enough to make it the usual answer to enemy siege, Trebuchets included, though the splash hurts your own units too. The Chinese invented the cannon in real life, yet their in-game civilization cannot build it for balance reasons.
boyar: The Slavic take on the Knight, with several times the melee armor of the Knight line. That armor wears out light units that rely on plain hits, like light cavalry and Eagle Warriors, and even the first Boyar fights in melee about as well as a Cavalier. It is a little slower than a Knight and falls to the same counters, Monks above all, since the Slavs lack Heresy. Boyars were the top rank of Slavic and Balkan nobility below the ruling princes.
camel-archer: A Berber mounted archer on a camel, built to beat other mounted archers with its bonus damage against them. Because it counts as a camel unit, anti-cavalry bonuses barely touch it: Camel Riders deal much less bonus damage and Mamelukes none at all. It also handles infantry and can trade with most foot archers, which makes it a flexible core for a Berber cavalry army. The sword on its side is only for show.
camel-rider: Camel Riders hunt cavalry. Their bonus against horses is unusually high for the Castle Age, and camels are the third fastest land units in the game, so they can chase down and finish the cavalry that Pikemen only scare away. At equal numbers they win most duels against melee cavalry, and they can force fights with mounted archers. Their availability follows geography: camels went to war between the Mediterranean and India.
camel-scout: The Gurjaras start with a Camel Scout instead of Scout Cavalry. It scouts just as well and wins a straight duel with an enemy scout, though its weak opening attack is useless for killing the enemy's sheep. After the first age-up it gains a large bonus against cavalry and becomes an anti-scout unit, handy in team games where it can kill two Scout Cavalry in a row. It is the only unique unit that turns into a regular one, the Camel Rider.
cannon-galleon: Think of it as a Bombard Cannon on water. It outranges Castles and Bombard Towers, so it can shell buildings along the shore from beyond their reach, while slow shots and a minimum range leave it nearly helpless against other ships. It needs Galleons or Fire Ships around it to survive. Spanish Cannon Galleons are far better than everyone else's, since their cannonballs fly fast and lead moving targets without Ballistics.
capped-ram: The Battering Ram with a metal cap on its head, which makes it hit buildings harder and gives it splash damage against nearby structures and units, so massed walls and packed bases fall much faster. Arrows barely scratch it, while melee units and Villagers tear it apart. Infantry riding inside make it faster and stronger against buildings. It is mostly a stepping stone to the Siege Ram, but the upgrade is cheap enough to be almost always worth taking.
caravel: This Portuguese warship fires bolts that pass through every unit in a line, so the tighter the enemy is packed, the more it hurts. One Caravel loses to a War Galley, yet a fleet of them beats a fleet of War Galleys or Galleons, and near the shore it shoots into clumps of land units like a floating Scorpion. Forcing the enemy to chase bunches its ships up. Columbus sailed two caravels, the Nina and the Pinta, in 1492.
cataphract: The Byzantine heavy cavalry is built to fight infantry. A big bonus against foot soldiers plus trample damage lets it cut through infantry blobs, and its extra armor against anti-cavalry bonuses means Camel Riders and Mamelukes barely get their bonus in, while even Halberdiers lose half of theirs. Low pierce armor leaves it exposed to archers, and it needs its late upgrades to shine. With fewer weaknesses than most unique units, it makes a good first unique unit for new players.
cavalier: The upgraded Knight, and for many civilizations the last step of the line. It raids, flanks and stands in front of archers and siege as a meat shield, all a bit better than the Knight did. Even civilizations that can go on to the Paladin often stay with Cavaliers, because they give more for the gold when gold runs short, especially in 1v1. Historically "cavalier" was just a general word for any knight; the game turns it into a rank.
cavalry-archer: Archers on horseback, one of the best harassers in the game and a natural answer to slow infantry. They reward constant micro: kept at a distance, a small group can wipe out whole formations of foot soldiers. Getting them going is expensive because they need a long list of technologies before they hit hard. This was the Mongol style of war, striking and withdrawing and avoiding hand-to-hand fighting until the enemy was demoralized.
centurion: A Roman heavy cavalryman that outfights a Knight in melee and takes more crossbow fire. Its real worth is Imperium, an aura that makes nearby Militia line units move and attack faster, so Romans often keep a few Centurions behind their Legionaries as support. They are expensive and slow to mass, and Monks are a serious danger because the Romans have no Heresy. A converted Centurion boosts the swordsmen of whoever converted it.
chakram-thrower: Gurjara infantry that throw metal discs which fly through every enemy in a straight line, like a Scorpion bolt. Each hit is weak, so the damage comes from lining up targets, and a tight group firing into packed infantry can in theory bring down even heavily armored foot soldiers in a few volleys. That makes them one of the most micro-intensive units in the game, since an opponent who spreads out takes most of the sting away.
champi-runner: South American civilizations have no horses, so their early raiding falls to this mace-carrying runner. It plays like a Man-at-Arms crossed with an Eagle Scout: quick, far-sighted and tougher against arrows than the Militia line, though weaker in a straight melee. A dozen of them with a few Skirmishers makes a typical raiding party, and they can even build Outposts. Each of the four civilizations gives it a twist; Tupi Runners, for example, refund part of their cost when they die.
champi-scout: An infantry scout that the Inca, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi start the game with instead of a mounted one. It is quick, shrugs off arrows better than a Militia, and unlike Militia or Eagle Scouts it can build Outposts. A few of them make a decent early rush to disrupt the enemy economy and stop early walls, though they fare worse than Militia against other melee units. It is the only starting scout that can be upgraded in the Feudal Age.
champi-warrior: The basic infantry of the South American civilizations, filling the Long Swordsman's slot with the speed and arrow resistance of an Eagle Warrior. For the Inca, Muisca and Tupi it is the best raider they have, and it handles siege and most archers well, while heavy cavalry and other infantry beat it. Like the Champi Runner it can build Outposts. Each civilization gets its own version: Muisca ones heal at Settlements, and Tupi ones refund part of their cost when they die.
champion: Few infantry units hit as hard as the Champion, and it is the usual late-game way to beat trash, since Halberdiers, Elite Skirmishers and Hussars all lose to it. That earned it the nickname trash buster, and it pairs well with rams for razing a town. During development the designers got tired of waiting for its art and had a coder put a floating "H" over the unit; when the artists saw it, they stayed late to finish the job.
chu-ko-nu: A repeating crossbow that fires a burst of bolts with every shot. Only the first bolt hits at full strength, yet the extras add up against units with no pierce armor such as Monks, and an engine quirk makes each one hurt rams far more than it should. Other archers can kite it, so it works best massed behind a melee line. Despite the name, Zhuge Liang did not invent the weapon; it was in use two centuries before his birth.
composite-bowman: Armenian archers whose arrows ignore the pierce armor of every land unit except siege. Huskarls, Ghulams and Rattan Archers, built to shrug off arrows, take full damage, and cavalry suffers badly too. The price is a short range, the same as a mounted archer's, so other foot archers can kite them and siege weapons still hurt. Their arrows fly straight instead of arcing, as they did in the first Age of Empires, so they hit targets running straight at or away from them.
condottiero: An Italian mercenary on foot whose job is killing gunpowder units. Special armor cancels the bonus damage that Hand Cannoneers, Organ Guns and Grenadiers deal to infantry, and it hits gunpowder units hard in return. It comes fully upgraded the moment the Imperial Age arrives, which makes it a quick answer to a fast Imperial gunpowder push and a strong choice for landings on water maps, where the defender rarely has upgraded troops. The historical condottieri were mercenary captains who mostly fought on horseback.
conquistador: Think of the Conquistador as a Hand Cannoneer on horseback that swaps the bonus against infantry for speed and toughness. Few technologies affect it, so it is ready to fight as soon as it is trained, and an early Conquistador rush catches unprepared opponents badly. Its range is the shortest of any gunpowder unit, which pushes it into hit-and-run play with heavy volleys into enemy formations. Monks are its worst enemy, since they can land conversions on an expensive unit before going down.
coustillier: Burgundian horsemen built around one big opening blow. The first strike against a unit carries a heavy charge bonus that takes a while to refill, and fresh Coustilliers leave the Castle fully charged. That makes them deadly at hit and run, against archers and on raids, while in a long slugging match the Knight line does better. The name comes from the coustille, a short sword, and the first coustilliers were professional French foot soldiers serving alongside a knight.
crossbowman: The upgraded Archer and, with the Knight, the classic power unit of the middle game. Crossbowmen get stronger the more of them there are: a big enough group kills melee units before they arrive and can drop Knights in a single volley. They do little to buildings, so attacks pair them with melee infantry, and Mangonels are their main threat. According to the manual, a peasant with a few hours of crossbow practice could kill a knight who had trained all his life.
demolition-raft: A Petard on water: a raft packed with explosives that sails into enemy ships and blows up. As the fastest warship of the Feudal Age it can run down a clump of Galleys or Fire Galleys and trade one raft for several of them. Because it destroys itself when it wins, it works best as support for a fleet that survives to hold the water. Rafts hidden in a Dock can burst out on ships that come too close.
demolition-ship: A Petard on water: the Demolition Ship sails into its target and blows up, hitting everything in the blast without harming friendly ships. As the fastest military ship it can chase down a loaded Transport Ship or dive into a clump of Galleys, and the blast goes off at full strength even if the owner detonates it early. Opponents tend to shoot at them first, which lets Fire Ships close in. As the core of a navy it falls flat, wasted on cheap targets.
dragon-ship: The Chinese version of the Fast Fire Ship, a flamethrower boat that has to get right up against its target. It gives up a little toughness for more damage, slightly more reach and extra speed, which helps it chase enemy ships or escape a bad fight. It works as a front line that soaks Galleon fire and ties up enemy fire ships. In the HD Edition it carried a dragon figurehead, but the Definitive Edition gave it a bird instead.
dromon: A siege ship that does the Cannon Galleon's job without gunpowder, which gives the Romans and Huns a long range warship even though their history ended before cannons. It outranges most Castles, Keeps and Bombard Towers, so it can strip a shoreline of buildings from safety. Its shorter range, wider blast and faster shots also make it better against other ships than a Cannon Galleon, though it still needs an escort and cannot hit anything up close.
eagle-scout: The Aztecs and Maya have no horses, so they scout on foot with the Eagle Scout. It is slower than a Scout Cavalry but sees further and fights better, which makes it the best scout of the Dark Age, and in the Feudal Age it allows an Eagle rush because nothing cheap counters it yet. It also hunts Monks and siege, though most infantry deal bonus damage to it. Real Eagle Warriors were high ranking Aztec soldiers; the actual scouts were called quimichtin, "mice".
eagle-warrior: Aztec and Maya armies have no cavalry, and the Eagle Warrior fills that gap as a fast infantry scout with long sight and resistance to conversion. It raids, hunts Monks and siege and handles foot archers well, while nearly every other infantry unit deals bonus damage to it. The historical Aztec Eagle and Jaguar Warriors were equal ranks with the same military job; the game turned the Eagles into scouts to stand in for cavalry.
elephant-archer: The toughest archer in the game, a bowman on an elephant who shoots no harder than a Cavalry Archer. Its worth is in population: a pack of them holds far more hit points per slot than any other ranged army and survives Mangonel shots that would wipe out foot archers. Being both an elephant and a mounted archer leaves it with a long list of counters. Oddly, its arrows fly out of the elephant's head instead of the rider's bow.
elite-battle-elephant: Slow, heavy elephants that trample everything around their target, which pays off more the bigger the battle gets. They crush most melee units, soak arrow fire for a long time and make a good wall for friendly archers, though they are too slow to raid. Every civilization with them adds a bonus or unique technology, so no generic version exists: Khmer elephants hit harder than any other Stable unit, and Vietnamese ones carry the most hit points after the War Elephant.
elite-cannon-galleon: A Bombard Cannon on water, and the ship with the longest range in the game. It outranges Castles and Bombard Towers, so its job is clearing the shoreline of buildings that would otherwise sink ships. Its shots are slow to fire and slow to travel, which makes it nearly useless against moving ships, and it needs Fire Ships or Galleons as an escort. Spanish ones are the exception: their cannonballs fly more than twice as fast and lead moving targets.
elite-champi-warrior: For the Inca, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi this is the everyday late-game infantry, a quick, archer-resistant generalist somewhere between the Militia line and the Eagle Warrior that can also build Outposts. Its speed and armor against arrows make it the best raider most of these civilizations have. The real champi warriors carried maces of stone, copper or even gold and wore cotton or llama wool armor that stopped arrows and sling stones.
elite-eagle-warrior: For the Aztecs and Maya the Eagle line does the job other civilizations give to cavalry, and the Elite version is the fastest infantry in the game. It scouts, raids, hunts Monks and siege, and handles light cavalry thanks to its bonus against mounted units, though heavy cavalry and other infantry are another matter. The two civilizations use it differently: Aztec Eagles hit hard enough to kill Villagers quickly, while Mayan ones carry far more hit points for pitched battles.
elite-elephant-archer: The toughest archer in the game, and the first unit to lose its unique status: it belonged to the Indians before it became a regional unit. It hits no harder than a Heavy Cavalry Archer, so its value lies in survival and population efficiency, taking several Onager shots that would kill ordinary archers outright. The Dravidian version is the most dangerous, firing faster than any other archer in the game.
elite-fire-lancer: Gunpowder shock infantry for the Chinese and their neighbors, and the only infantry in the game that costs no food. In melee it is a decent cavalry killer, and when its charge is ready it fires an inaccurate volley of fire lance shots that ignore armor, which works best against massed, slow infantry. With hit and run it can even kite heavy infantry that it should never meet head on. Its weapon is drawn from a fire lance illustration in the Wubei Zhi.
elite-skirmisher: The Elite Skirmisher is a trash unit built to shoot down archers. Bonus damage against foot archers and Cavalry Archers plus thick pierce armor let it win ranged fights far above its price, and its bonus against the Spearman line helps in trash wars. One or two do almost nothing, so it gets massed, especially late when gold runs out. The Swiss sometimes used up to a quarter of their army as skirmishers to screen their pikemen.
elite-steppe-lancer: The upgraded Steppe Lancer keeps its odd trick of striking from just behind the front rank, so a mass of them can stab over a line of Cavaliers or trash units. The reach also lets several gang up on one Villager or siege weapon at once, which makes them quick raiders, though one on one they lose to heavy cavalry. Early versions could stack into tiny clumps, and lobby hosts used to kick Cuman players until a patch fixed it.
elite-varangian-guard: A heavy generalist infantryman that earns gold for its owner whenever it fights enemy units, so a long brawl partly pays for itself. Next to a Champion it is tougher, hits harder and moves faster, but it costs more and has no bonus damage. The unit recalls the mercenaries who guarded the Byzantine emperor, drawn from Scandinavia, England and the lands of the Rus', who went home rich after their service.
fast-fire-ship: The Imperial Age Fire Ship, whose bow flamethrower only works right next to its target. Up close it beats a Galleon, but a fleet of Galleons wins at range, so Fast Fire Ships do best inside a mixed fleet that lets them close in and burn through enemy Galleons. Demolition Ships and Turtle Ships, which also fight up close, are their worst enemies. Along with the Fire Ship, it is the only unit that deals melee and pierce damage at once.
fire-archer: Wu's Fire Archer changes its attack by target. Against buildings and ships it fires a single long shot that outranges even upgraded Castles and towers, so the Wu can siege down fortifications from safety long before Trebuchets are around. Against units it looses three short-range arrows in a row, each with a small blast that spares friendly troops. In an open fight it does clearly worse than the same number of Crossbowmen. Oddly, it uses its anti-building shot on animals.
fire-galley: Before this ship existed, early naval fights were simply Galleys shooting Galleys. The Fire Galley sprays flame at close range, and its heavy pierce armor lets it beat Galleys in any numbers, so it is usually the main warship early on water maps and can even raze an enemy Dock. Its flames can be blocked by units or buildings standing between it and the target, and Hulks punish it hard. The design draws on the Byzantine dromon and its Greek fire.
fire-lancer: An anti-cavalry infantryman that opens each fight with a short range gunpowder volley that ignores armor, then wades into melee. That opening shot gives it an edge over Pikemen against heavily armored horsemen, and it also beats the Spearman line outright. It is the only Barracks unit that costs no food, which suits civilizations whose economy already runs on wood and gold for archers or siege, though the gold cost and longer training make it less disposable than a Pikeman.
fire-ship: A ship with a flamethrower on the bow that sprays fire about four times a second at point blank range. Heavy anti-ship armor lets it close in under fire and tear through most ships, the Hulk line aside. It works as support next to War Galleys or Galleons and as an escort for Transport Ships, since its short reach leaves it open to Demolition Ships. The design comes from Byzantine dromons with Greek fire siphons, though the game leaves off their oars.
fishing-ship: Fishing Ships are the economy on water. On deep-sea fish close to a Dock they gather food faster than a Villager on a Farm, and they can build Fish Traps, water Farms that hold more food but gather more slowly than wild fish. They also bring in gold from Oysters and Whales and share the Villager's Drop Off button. With no attack, they cannot defend themselves against enemy warships.
flaming-camel: A Tatar camel loaded with burning straw that charges into the enemy and explodes. The blast is built for elephants and cavalry, so a few of these thrown into a packed group of War Elephants or Elephant Archers can wreck it. Nothing raises its armor, arrows kill it fast, and against buildings it is far weaker than a Petard. The idea comes from Tamerlane, who used flaming camels to panic the Indian war elephants at Delhi in 1398.
flemish-militia: Burgundian town militia armed with the goedendag, a cheap weapon that worked well against horsemen. It beats most foot soldiers in melee while keeping bonus damage against cavalry, and instead of an Elite upgrade it grows stronger by itself with each new age. Flemish Revolution turns every Burgundian Villager into Flemish Militia, who can no longer gather or build. Doing that to 50 Villagers earns the Golden Spurs achievement, named after the 1302 battle where Flemish infantry cut down French cavalry.
galleon: The standard late game warship for nearly every civilization and the backbone of an Imperial Age navy. Galleons win through numbers, sinking enemy Galleons and Demolition Ships in groups and pounding units and buildings near the shore, and they pair well with Fire Ships. Towers, Castles and heavy warships like the Turtle Ship are what give them trouble. The name is a little off: real galleons never carried ballistae, and the Cannon Galleon is closer to the historical ship.
galley: The Galley is a small, fast warship used to scout the water and hunt Fishing Ships and anything else near the shore. One or two achieve little, while a fleet sinks ships with ease. Fire Galleys usually beat them, so Galleys tend to become the main warship only after the War Galley upgrade, though they keep a niche in shore bombardment. Despite the name they run on a single sail, which makes them closer to a sloop than a galley.
gbeto: Malian knife throwers who deal melee damage from range, which lets them cut through units with heavy pierce armor such as Huskarls, Elite Skirmishers and rams. They are fast enough to hit and run on almost any infantry, and they pair well with light cavalry that takes the hits they cannot. Gbeto means "huntress" in the Fon language, and the unit is based on the women warriors of Dahomey, who were never part of the Mali Empire.
genitour: A Skirmisher on horseback that costs no gold, so the Berbers can keep making it when gold runs dry. It beats almost every archer unit in the game, the Genoese Crossbowman being the exception, and it makes a decent Monk deterrent because a converted one is of little use to the enemy. It is also the Berber team bonus, so every ally can train it, which may echo the Zenata horsemen who fought for whichever ruler paid them.
genoese-crossbowman: An Italian crossbowman with a real bonus against cavalry, elephants and camels, so where most archers merely survive cavalry, massed Genoese Crossbowmen beat it. The bonus covers ships as well: two Elite Genoese Crossbowmen can sink a fully upgraded Galleon that would take about ten Arbalesters. The historical Genoese worked in teams of three, one holding the pavise shield, one reloading a spare crossbow and one shooting, which roughly doubled their rate of fire.
ghulam: Infantry usually die on the walk to an archer line, and the Ghulam gets there thanks to its speed and high pierce armor, then adds a bonus against archers. Its spear thrust also hits the unit behind the target, so clumped archers suffer most, and since the Hindustanis have no Knights it doubles as their raider. The real ghilman were slave soldiers used as a swift strike force before the main army engaged, though they usually fought on horseback.
grenadier: Jurchen bomb throwers, best described as a Mangonel on legs with poor aim. Their exploding iron balls tear through clumps of infantry and archers that a Hand Cannoneer would pick off one at a time, and they hurt friendly units too, although Jurchen troops take only half of that. They need numbers and a screen in front, because cavalry and siege reach them easily. With Thunderclap Bombs they also blow up when they die, which punishes anything that closes in.
guecha-warrior: Muisca javelin throwers that play like a faster, harder hitting Skirmisher with less range. When one dies, nearby Guecha Warriors regain some health, so a big group is hard to wear down. Their speed lets them hit and run against slow infantry and raid Villagers the way mounted archers do, without taking anti-cavalry bonus damage. Historically they were the elite warriors of the Muisca and often carried mummified ancestors into battle.
halberdier: The Imperial Age spearman, a cheap unit with no gold cost whose bonus against cavalry is so large that two Halberdiers can bring down a Paladin. It cannot chase anything, so it stands guard over archers and siege that would otherwise get run over. Late in the game, when gold runs dry and armies turn into trash units, it keeps Hussars in check. It is weak against everything else, so it works in numbers next to other units.
hand-cannoneer: Hand Cannoneers fire slow, heavy shots that tear through infantry and large cavalry, though at long range their bullets fly off in random directions. They count as archers for bonus damage as well as gunpowder units, so Skirmishers, Huskarls and Ghulams all get bonuses against them. Their food cost makes them awkward in a normal economy, and they usually turn up in special builds such as a Fast Imperial on closed maps. The Chinese invented the hand cannon, yet they cannot train it.
heavy-camel-rider: The upgraded Camel Rider is built for killing cavalry. Against horsemen it hits about as hard as a Halberdier while being far tougher, and its speed lets it force fights and run down mounted archers that spearmen could never catch. Against infantry, foot archers or buildings it has little to offer. Camels are one of the few units whose spread among civilizations matches history well, since armies from the Mediterranean to India really fought on them.
heavy-cavalry-archer: The armored Cavalry Archer, fast enough to hit and run and sturdy enough to survive when caught. It only pays off in large numbers, which makes it an expensive army to build, and the upgrade's jump in accuracy matters most for civilizations without Thumb Ring. The classic pairing is with Hussars: the archers spend wood and gold while the Hussars spend food and screen them. According to the manual, the Byzantines used heavy cavalry archers extensively against Persian and steppe horsemen.
heavy-demolition-ship: The last and largest of the explosive boats, sinking most ships it rams in one blast; only the Trebuchet deals more base damage. Together with the Demolition Ship it is the fastest military vessel in the game, a fine answer to Fire Ships and a disaster for a loaded Transport Ship. It also explodes when killed, without ever hurting friendly units. Since every attack costs the ship, it supports a navy and cannot carry one.
heavy-hei-guang-cavalry: Shu, Wei and Wu have no Knights, and the Heavy Hei Guang Cavalry takes the same job as all-purpose heavy cavalry that runs down infantry, siege and light cavalry. Compared with the Cavalier it carries fewer hit points and more armor. Each of the three civilizations ends up with a different version: the Wei one is much tougher and gets a bonus against siege, while the Wu one hits hardest.
heavy-rocket-cart: This stand-in for the Onager, used by the Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans and Koreans, fires a salvo of rockets into an area, and each rocket ignores the armor of the units it hits. That makes it better than an Onager against packed groups of armored troops and worse against buildings with Masonry and Architecture. It can also attack the ground and clear trees. Korean carts with Shinkichon reach far enough to counter enemy Onagers.
heavy-scorpion: A heavier Scorpion whose bolts run through every unit in a line and never hurt your own troops, so it can fire freely into a crowded melee. A medium sized group can erase whole armies of infantry and archers, but fast units dodge the slow bolts and close in, so Halberdiers usually guard it. The original manual claimed it was good against massed cavalry and fortifications, which is close to the opposite of how it plays.
hei-guang-cavalry: The Three Kingdoms civilizations' version of the Knight, trading hit points for armor. That armor keeps it alive longer than expected in most fights, and a fully upgraded Wei one has the highest melee armor of any Stable unit. The low hit points hurt against Pikemen and Camel Riders, whose big bonuses cut through it, and it gets none of the technologies that boost the Knight line. Hei guang means "black brilliant", a type of armor from the Three Kingdoms period.
houfnice: The Bohemian upgrade of the Bombard Cannon has a bigger blast, more bonus damage against buildings and siege, and enough armor to soak more arrows. It also flips the duel with Siege Onagers: an Onager needs two shots to kill a Houfnice, while one Houfnice shot kills the Onager. At choke points on closed maps it was strong enough that it has been toned down several times. English gets the word howitzer from the Czech houfnice, which comes from houf, meaning crowd.
huskarl: Gothic infantry whose armor makes arrows almost useless against them, with bonus damage against archers and buildings on top. A Huskarl push can walk through an archer army and take down a Castle with little trouble, which makes them one of the best raiders in the game. In melee they are ordinary at best. The name comes from the retinues of Germanic chiefs, warriors who served their leader for a large share of the plunder.
hussar: The top of the Scout Cavalry line, a fast horseman that costs only food and keeps fighting after the gold is gone. It is weak in a straight fight, so its work is raiding, scouting and running down Monks, siege weapons and Elite Skirmishers. The classic army pairs them with mounted archers, who get the gold while the Hussars screen them. The name comes from the Hungarian light cavalry of the 15th century, though the model looks more like a Polish Winged Hussar.
hussite-wagon: A Bohemian war wagon that works as a moving shield. Enemy shots that pass through it reach the units behind at half strength, with the wagon taking the other half, so it rolls in front of Bohemian ranged units while firing a spread of bullets of its own. The real Hussite rebels of the 1420s used wagons like this to let a mostly peasant army hold off the Holy Roman Empire's knights.
ibirapema-warrior: The Tupi front line swings a heavy two-handed club that deals full damage to every enemy in a cone in front of it, so dense groups of infantry and lightly armored cavalry melt against a line of Ibirapema Warriors. It is tough for infantry and refunds part of its cost when it dies, though its gold price makes it hard to mass late. The ibirapema was a heavy wooden club that the Tupi also used in ritual sacrifice.
imperial-camel-rider: The Hindustanis' last step on the camel line, and the closest thing they have to heavy cavalry, since they lack the Knight line entirely. It keeps the camel's job of beating cavalry one on one, and with Hindustani bonuses to attack speed and damage against buildings it can also put real pressure on an enemy town. Foot units remain a problem. The upgrade strips the camel of its cloak, even though the upgrade icon shows a camel in armor.
imperial-skirmisher: The Vietnamese take the Elite Skirmisher one step further, and through their team bonus every ally can research it too. It costs no gold, so it stays useful deep into a late game, and it takes far less damage from Arbalesters while dealing more back. Against anything other than archers and Pikemen it does almost nothing. Unlike the other shared units, each ally has to research it separately at their own Archery Range.
iron-pagoda: The Jurchens have no Knights, and the Iron Pagoda fills that slot, coming out of a Castle faster than a Knight leaves a Stable. Its trick is a shield that blocks one melee hit completely before it recharges, which tips close fights its way and fully cancels the blast of suicide units like Flaming Camels and Demolition Ships. Projectiles ignore the shield. The unit carries a horse-chopping sword, the same weapon Song infantry used against the real Jin Iron Pagoda.
jaguar-warrior: The Aztec infantry killer has a bonus against foot soldiers big enough to beat any other infantry one on one except Teutonic Knights and Samurai. It also grows stronger in battle, gaining attack for each enemy military unit it kills, up to four. That cap mirrors the Aztec ranks, where a warrior had to take four captives to join the eagle and jaguar orders. Against armies that are not built around infantry, the Aztec Champion or Siege Onager usually does the job better.
janissary: The Turkish gunman, a longer-ranged Hand Cannoneer with no minimum range. Their volleys kill or cripple anything that gets too close, they handle infantry and buildings well, and they shred early siege, which is why a Castle drop into Janissaries is a favorite on Arena. Low accuracy and slow reloads leave them open to archers and fast units. The designers first planned them as heavy foot archers before turning them into gunpowder troops.
jian-swordsman: Wu swordsmen who fight behind a shield until they are badly hurt, then throw it away, trading arrow protection for more attack and speed. Once Wu regeneration heals them past the threshold, the shield comes back. With it raised, Crossbowmen barely scratch them, which makes an early raid into an archer town devastating. Their shock infantry class is the weak spot, and Long Swordsmen and Samurai cut them down.
kamayuk: An Inca spearman whose spear is long enough to strike past the man in front, so a packed block of Kamayuks fights with every soldier at once and can even stab over walls at rams. It cuts down cavalry, camels and elephants, and in large groups it holds its own against ordinary infantry, something Pikemen cannot do. With gold to spare, Inca players pick it over the Halberdier. In the Inca army a kamayuq was an officer in charge of lesser troops such as slingers.
karambit-warrior: Karambit Warriors are quantity over quality: cheap, quick and frail, and each takes only half a population slot. A swarm can raid Villagers, surround and hack down buildings away from towers, or rush out to kill rams in an emergency, while a few trickled into a fight just get picked off. It is the cheapest unit in the game in raw resources, and the idea very likely comes from the Zerglings of StarCraft.
keshik: Tatar medium cavalry that earns a slow trickle of gold while it fights enemy units, which helps keep a late game economy alive. It needs less gold than a Knight, takes arrows better than a Cavalier and keeps pace with mounted archers, so it makes a strong raider. It still loses to anti-cavalry and heavier horsemen, and Monks convert it easily. The name comes from the kheshig, the elite warriors Genghis Khan picked as his personal bodyguard.
king: The unit a Regicide game is played around: lose your King and you lose the match on the spot. He cannot fight or work, but he is quick, sees far and is ignored by wild animals, so he can scout around your own town early before hiding in the Castle every Regicide player starts with. He cannot be converted, yet unlike heroes he never regenerates. Almost every regional King is drawn as obese, except the Mesoamerican and South American ones.
kipchak: A Cuman horse archer that fires several arrows in each volley. Only the first arrow carries its full attack, but the extra arrows always do some damage, so the Kipchak keeps chipping away at targets that shrug off normal arrows, rams and Monks included. It is played like a Cavalry Archer, harassing slow units with hit and run, and its short attack delay makes the micro easy. With Cuman Mercenaries, every allied player gets a limited batch of free Elite Kipchaks at their Castles.
knight: For most civilizations the Knight is the main fighting force once it arrives, running down infantry, archers, siege and light cavalry and raiding villages with ease. It is strongest early, while counters are scarce, and loses ground as Pikemen, Camel Riders and massed Crossbowmen come in, though its upgrades stay relevant to the end. The first design gave it a lance, swapped for a sword before release, and its base stats have not changed once since the game came out.
kona: Mapuche horsemen that hit harder the more wounded their target already is, whoever did the wounding. That makes them a natural finisher next to Bolas Riders or archers that soften enemies first, and they also carry bonus damage against gunpowder units. With no melee armor and no cavalry armor upgrades in the Mapuche tree, they are glass cannons. The club in the Kona's left hand swings in the animation but never deals any damage.
konnik: A Bulgarian horseman with two lives: when the mounted Konnik dies, the rider gets up and fights on as infantry. The two forms have different weaknesses, so the Pikemen that beat the horse struggle against the man on foot, and the opponent needs two kinds of answer. Against Monks, players sometimes delete their own mounted Konniks on purpose, so the conversion has to start over while the dismounted rider runs at the Monk. The name simply means horseman in Bulgarian.
legionary: The Roman replacement for the Two-Handed Swordsman and the Champion, reached in a single upgrade that is cheaper and quicker than the two it skips. It hits infantry and buildings hard and beats Halberdiers, Elite Skirmishers and Hussars with ease, so it shines in the early Imperial Age and again once gold runs out. A nearby Centurion speeds up its movement and attacks. Because it counts as an upgraded Long Swordsman, the Samurai's bonus against unique units does not apply to it.
leitis: The Leitis ignores armor when it hits a unit, which leaves heavily armored opponents like Teutonic Knights and Boyars effectively naked and makes every armor upgrade the enemy buys a waste. Each Relic in a Lithuanian Monastery adds to its attack, and with all four it ranks among the hardest hitting non-siege units. It is faster but frailer than the Knight line. The name is a Latvian word for Lithuanians, later used for soldiers who answered only to the monarch.
liao-dao: Khitan heavy infantry whose blades leave enemies bleeding, and the bleed ignores armor and stacks. For equal resources the Liao Dao beats strong melee units such as Boyars and Teutonic Knights, and it stops regenerating units like Berserks from healing. Poor arrow protection and one of the slowest swings of any infantry mean it needs archers or siege covering it. The name comes from a weapon: Liao for the Khitan dynasty, dao for a Chinese blade.
light-cavalry: Fast, food-only horsemen made for scouting and chasing down Monks, siege weapons and Elite Skirmishers, with little to offer in a real melee. While gold is plentiful a Knight is usually the better fighter, but Light Cavalry grow more useful as gold runs out, both as raiders and as trash units. Oddly, it is the only unit that moves slower than the unit it upgrades from. It can later become either a Hussar or a Winged Hussar.
long-swordsman: The basic Castle Age infantry, light on gold and able to beat most standard Castle Age units one on one, the Knight and Cavalry Archer excepted. Slow and exposed to arrows, it mostly sees use against trash units, Camel Riders, Eagle Warriors and other shock infantry, or in numbers against Goths and their Huskarls. Two of them can beat a full health Knight. The name is a misnomer, since a real longsword is two-handed and this unit swings a one-handed arming sword.
longbowman: The Briton archer is all about range: a fully upgraded Elite Longbowman shoots farther than any other archer and can hit Castles, towers and Onagers from outside their reach. The Britons lack Thumb Ring, so the arrows miss more often, but strays still hurt nearby enemies and a focused volley wastes less damage on overkill. The real English longbow never outranged the Asian composite bow; the game stretches it for gameplay.
longship: Northern raiding ships that loose a spread of arrows at once, each arrow at full damage. They train quickly, need no Medium Warships upgrade and stack tightly, so the usual plan is to mass them early and sweep the enemy off the water. Tight stacks invite splash damage from Mangonels and Turtle Ships, though good micro dodges much of it. Until The Viking Sagas the unit was called Longboat, which is a different and much later kind of boat.
lou-chuan: Its name means tower ship, and it carries two weapons: a Traction Trebuchet on the prow for buildings and siege, and a tower of archers for everything else, switching between them on its own. Shots that miss still deal full damage, and it knocks down buildings faster than even an Elite Cannon Galleon. Leaving heroes aside, nothing in the game costs more wood and gold. Historically the tall tower made it top heavy, so it stayed on rivers and lakes.
magyar-huszar: A cheap, fast Magyar horseman made for killing siege weapons and raiding. It pairs naturally with Cavalry Archers, clearing away the Mangonels and Elite Skirmishers that trouble them, and after Corvinian Army it costs only food, which turns it into a trash unit. It rarely wins a straight melee fight, but it costs so little that it still trades well, and an Elite Magyar Huszar kills a Villager in fewer strikes than a Hussar. The bow on its side is only for show.
mameluke: The Mameluke is a camel rider that throws its scimitar from a short distance as a melee attack. Speed, that reach and a bonus against cavalry make a well controlled group very hard to answer, and the high price is the catch; for years it was one of the least used unique units because of it. The historical mamluks rode horses, and the game seats them on two-humped Bactrian camels, probably to tell them apart from ordinary Camel Riders.
man-at-arms: The first upgrade of the Militia and the standard early infantry rush. A handful of Men-at-Arms beats nearly anything the opponent has on the field that early, so they go after Villagers and buildings, usually with a few Skirmishers or Archers along to handle enemy archers. They are slow and fall behind once stronger units arrive, so the line needs upgrading as the game goes on. Historically the name fits a fully armored horseman better than a foot swordsman.
mangonel: The great equalizer of archer wars: one good shot into a clump of Crossbowmen can turn a battle, and at high level the main answer to a Mangonel is another Mangonel. It also outranges Town Centers and hurts buildings, so it is a common way to pressure an opponent. The blast hits your own units too, so it usually travels with archers or Monks and needs a careful hand. The model is a plain catapult, while a real mangonel was a small trebuchet.
mangudai: The Mongol horse archer, tougher than a Cavalry Archer and easier to micro thanks to a short attack delay. It hunts slow targets such as Monks, Villagers and infantry, picks off archers caught off guard, and its bonus against siege lets it kill rams from behind walls. The historical Mangudai were the vanguard of the Mongol army, named after the Manghud clan, and they rode small, almost pony-sized Mongolian horses, while the game gives them full warhorses.
militia: Militia are the only soldiers available at the very start, and their main job is the drush: a small band runs into the enemy base, with the scout blocking fleeing Villagers, to disrupt the economy and stop the opponent from walling. Killing Villagers matters less than slowing the enemy down, and Villagers with Loom can fight back. Against buildings and upgraded units they do almost nothing. Although they belong to the sword line, they carry an iron club.
missionary: A Spanish Monk on horseback. It converts and heals like a Monk, but its speed lets it run from almost anything except other cavalry, and cavalry technologies such as Bloodlines make it tougher. In exchange it has a shorter conversion range and takes bonus damage from spearmen and camels. Converting a hundred units with Missionaries unlocks the achievement "Unexpected", a nod to Monty Python's Spanish Inquisition sketch.
monaspa: Georgian heavy cavalry that gets stronger in a crowd, gaining attack for every seven Monaspas or Knights nearby. Next to a Knight it hits harder, moves faster and has more melee armor, but far fewer hit points, so it is the damage dealer while Knights do the tanking, and it trains quickly enough to mass. Massed Elite Monaspas are a big reason the Georgians are often banned in tournaments, and the unit has been toned down several times.
monk: A Monk cannot fight, but it can take the enemy's army for you: one converted Knight or War Elephant pays for the Monk even if it dies a moment later. Monks also heal and carry Relics to the Monastery, where each Relic earns a slow stream of gold. Conversions never happen on their own, so Monks demand constant attention and get hard to use in a large Imperial Age battle. Now and then a Monk chants the old "Wololo" from the first game while converting.
mounted-trebuchet: Despite the name, the Khitan Mounted Trebuchet behaves like a camel-mounted Bombard Cannon: it goes for units before buildings and cannot outrange Castles. Each shot leaves a patch of fire that keeps burning enemies and ignores armor, and since it moves faster than a cannon and needs no Chemistry, it is a handy early answer to enemy siege. The design comes from the Tangut Boxi regiment, whose camels carried small catapults or staff slings on their backs.
obuch: Polish infantry with a hammer-pick that strips a point of armor with every hit, and the loss lasts until the target heals to full. The Obuch wears down heavily armored enemies such as Teutonic Knights and Serjeants and leaves them open to the Arbalesters and Winged Hussars behind it. It hits softer than a Champion yet outlasts one. The game shows a nadziak with an outward beak; a real obuch curved inward, and Polish nobles carried it like a cane.
onager: The upgraded Mangonel hits harder, throws further and can smash through trees, which lets it fire from behind a forest on maps like Black Forest. Archers and slow, packed units suffer most from it, but it cannot defend itself once melee units reach it, so Halberdiers or Monks usually guard it against cavalry. The name comes from the Greek for wild ass, since the engine was said to throw rocks as hard as the animal kicked.
organ-gun: A Portuguese volley gun that sprays a cone of light bullets, each tending to hit a different target. That shreds masses of lightly armored foot soldiers and does little to anything with good pierce armor. It has a minimum range and fires slowly, so Halberdiers or Hand Cannoneers should stand in front of it. The real weapon, the ribauldequin, was a row of small iron barrels on a wooden platform, and it took the name organ gun from its likeness to a pipe organ.
paladin: The Paladin is the last stage of the Knight line, and a big group of them can flatten an unprepared town or army. The upgrade is expensive enough that it only pays off when Paladins will carry the army, and their gold cost makes them a favorite target for enemy Monks. Few civilizations get it, and at times it has been the most exclusive non-regional unit in the game. The name comes from the legendary Twelve Peers of Charlemagne.
petard: A soldier with an explosive charge who runs at the target and blows himself up. Two of them bring down a section of Stone Wall, and they also work on enemy siege, though the tiny blast and frail body let ranged units pick them off on the way. Against a Castle, stagger them so each arrow volley hits only one. The name comes from a French word for breaking wind, and a bombardier whose charge went off early was "hoisted by his own petard".
pikeman: The cheap answer to cavalry: no gold, and enough bonus damage to cut down Knights, camels and elephants. Outside that job it is frail and weak, so Pikemen work in groups, as a screen for siege weapons or as cannon fodder. They cannot force a fight on fast cavalry that refuses to engage, which is why civilizations with camels often prefer Camel Riders against Knights. The weapon they actually carry is a glaive-guisarme, with a broad blade and a hook.
plumed-archer: This Maya archer is fast enough to keep up with some cavalry and far tougher than other foot archers, so it plays the hit and run role that a Cavalry Archer fills elsewhere, and players often call it the Native American Cavalry Archer. Its bonus against infantry handles most foot soldiers, and the Maya discount makes it cheap for what it is. On release a Fast Castle into Plumed Archers was the default Maya plan and a large part of their fearsome reputation.
ratha: The Bengalis have neither Knights nor Cavalry Archers, and the Ratha covers both: a chariot that switches with a button between a bow and a sword, with a little splash in sword mode. It keeps the archer armor classes even in melee, so Skirmishers hurt it badly, and fully upgrading both modes takes more technologies than any other unit. A mode-switching unit had already been tried for the Samurai and a Persian unit during the original game's development.
rattan-archer: Vietnamese foot archers with pierce armor close to a Huskarl's, so enemy arrows, Scorpion bolts and tower fire barely hurt them. They are also among the fastest foot archers, quick enough to chase retreating archers, raid Villagers under tower fire and even dodge Mangonel shots while picking at the Mangonel. Anything that reaches them in melee, cavalry above all, cuts them down, so they want an escort of elephants or infantry.
rocket-cart: A cart of rockets that takes the Mangonel's place for the Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans and Koreans. Each volley showers the target area with rockets that ignore the armor of non-siege land units, so it does more than a Mangonel against packed, armored troops, but its many small hits do poorly against buildings with Masonry. It is based on the Chinese nest of bees, an early multiple rocket launcher, and the Korean hwacha was a similar weapon.
samurai: The Samurai's bonus against other unique units makes it a hunter of enemy Castle units, and it grows more useful as the late game fills up with them. With the Japanese infantry bonus it ties for the fastest attacking infantry in the game, and it speeds up and builds a charged hit as it runs at a nearby enemy, which helps it close on archers and siege. Real early medieval samurai were mostly mounted archers, and the developers first gave this unit a bow before dropping the idea.
savar: The Persian replacement for the Paladin gives up some hit points for extra armor, a bonus against archers and a faster attack, and its upgrade is cheaper and quicker to research. That makes it far better than a Paladin at running down archers, and a large group crushes infantry, siege and unguarded towns. The Persians lack Heresy, so enemy Monks are a real danger. The Savar is modeled on the Sasanian Aswaran, the same source as the Byzantine Cataphract.
scorpion: A giant crossbow whose bolts pass through every unit in a line, hurting all of them and never harming your own troops. Used in numbers it is a strong answer to slow, packed infantry and archers, often behind Pikemen who keep cavalry off it. Fast cavalry dodges the bolts, and Mangonels are its usual counter. The original manual praised it against cavalry and fortifications, and in play it turned out to be weak at both.
scout-cavalry: The horseman most civilizations start with and the eyes of the opening, finding sheep, resources and the enemy base while its attack is still too weak to matter. Reaching the Feudal Age makes it faster and stronger for free, and from then on it raids Villagers and archers, moving faster than its own Light Cavalry and Hussar upgrades. Later it is a standard answer to Monk and siege pushes on closed maps like Arena.
serjeant: A heavily armored Sicilian infantryman that can build and repair Donjons, small fortresses that train more Serjeants. That allows the Donjon rush: a few Villagers raise one Donjon near the enemy in the Feudal Age, and its Serjeants then build more next to the enemy's mines and Lumber Camp. Later Serjeants serve as the Sicilian main infantry, trading attack for armor that holds up against arrows and swords alike. The name comes from serjeanty, land held in return for a duty other than knight service.
shotel-warrior: Shotel Warriors hit extremely hard for their cost, run fast and train in seconds, so they work as raiders and as an instant defense. A small group kills Villagers in two strikes, can level an unguarded Town Center quickly and keeps rams away from a forward Castle, though with almost no armor they die fast. The Elite version is the fastest training unit in the game. The curved shotel could reach around a shield or hook a rider off his horse.
shrivamsha-rider: Gurjara horsemen with a second, regenerating bar that lets them dodge a few projectiles outright, however hard each one hits. That makes them a menace to archers and raiders that towers struggle to stop, and they are nearly the fastest land unit in the game, quick enough to catch Trade Carts. Melee attacks ignore the dodge, and their plain stats are weak for the price. Shrivamsha was a horse breed said to cross seas of sand, a gift to King Mihira Bhoja.
siege-elephant: The South Asian civilizations' ram: an armored elephant built to knock down buildings, which shrugs off arrows and splashes damage onto everything around it, units included. Because it counts as cavalry, Monks heal it from a safe distance instead of Villagers repairing it at the front, and it can garrison in a Castle. Left alone, it also chases units it cannot beat. In ancient India, elephants trained to batter walls and gates did the work of rams.
siege-onager: The final Mangonel upgrade and arguably the deadliest siege weapon against units. Its larger blast is harder to dodge, and a few good shots into a dense pack of archers or slow units can turn a game. The rocks hurt friendly troops too, so it is usually guarded by Halberdiers or archers who stay clear of the blast. It can also smash trees, letting an army cut through a forest on maps like Black Forest.
siege-ram: The Siege Ram is the best ram for knocking down buildings and soaking up arrows. Up to six foot units can ride inside, and garrisoned infantry make it faster and hit buildings harder, so it works best next to infantry that keeps enemy melee units off it. It is also very good at killing Trebuchets. With the Mongol technology Drill, a fully garrisoned Siege Ram moves as fast as a starting Scout Cavalry.
siege-tower: The only military unit in the game that cannot attack. Its one job is to carry foot soldiers or Villagers to an enemy wall and drop them on the other side, and arrows barely hurt it on the way. It only pays off against a fully walled base, a second layer of walls stops it, and melee units tear it apart. To unload over the wall you order it to attack the wall section; ungarrisoning just drops the troops next to the tower.
skirmisher: A cheap javelin thrower whose only real job is killing archers, which it does well thanks to high pierce armor and bonus damage. It costs no gold, so it stays relevant in late games when gold runs out, and enough of them can swamp an opponent through sheer numbers. It barely scratches anything else. Medieval skirmishers were mostly armed with crossbows and longbows, so Javelineer would describe this unit better.
slinger: Slingers are the only real answer the South American civilizations have to infantry and Monks. They cost no gold, deal bonus damage to infantry, Monks and siege, and handle shock infantry best with Champi Warriors in front. Each civilization gets its own version: Inca Slingers can lose their minimum range, and Muisca ones can outrange a Heavy Scorpion. Historically slingers fought all over the Americas while Eagle Warriors were Aztec only, and the game reverses that.
spearman: Spearmen are the cheap, gold-free answer to cavalry. Large bonus damage against horses, camels and elephants lets them stop an early Scout rush and keep raiders out of the base, while their stats are poor against everything else; an unupgraded Spearman even loses to a Villager with Loom. Slow and without range, they defend and do not raid. Medieval armies used dense blocks of spearmen for the same reason, because horses would not charge into a wall of spear points.
steppe-lancer: Light cavalry with a lance long enough to strike from the second rank, so a mass of Steppe Lancers can fight over the backs of Knights in front of them. The reach lets many of them hit one target at once, which makes them unusually fast at tearing down Palisade Walls and buildings, and only light cavalry and camels can outrun them. After early nerfs they almost vanished from competitive play, then returned as Fast Castle strategies grew popular.
tarkan: Hunnic medium cavalry, somewhere between Light Cavalry and a Knight, whose real job is wrecking buildings. Tarkans raid towns and forward camps, knock down towers and other defenses with ease and have enough pierce armor to deal with the archers who come to stop them. They also help at home against a mass of enemy siege. The title tarkan was used by the Göktürks and the Bulgarian Khanate, but there is no record of it among the European Huns.
temple-guard: A Muisca shock infantryman that speeds up the longer it fights, because every hit shortens its next reload for a few seconds. That makes it good against durable targets such as elephants, Boyars and Paladins, and it is the Muisca answer to cavalry and a strong building breaker. It is one of only two military units that a Monastery can train, which helps when guarding Relics. The Elite version wears a gold mask modeled on Muisca goldwork.
teutonic-knight: The Teutonic Knight is the strongest infantry in the game, with the highest melee armor of any unit, and it beats almost anything in a slugging match, Paladins included. Its problem is speed: it is slower than nearly every unit outside siege and Monks, so ranged units kite it and opponents simply walk away. The real Teutonic Knights almost always fought on horseback; the game probably put them on foot so they would not resemble the Paladin.
thirisadai: A Dravidian battleship that fires a spread of arrows and carries armor that cancels the usual anti-ship bonus damage. It beats Galleons for the same resources, packs the value of two Galleons into one population slot and needs no upgrades, so it hits hard while other navies are still waiting on research. It is slow, and Fire Ships and Demolition Ships can outmaneuver it. Its name probably came from a Wikipedia article on the Chola navy whose claims later turned out to be fabricated.
throwing-axeman: Frankish infantry that throw axes, so they deal melee damage from range: they stand behind the front line like archers while being countered like infantry. Few units have more melee armor than pierce armor, so the axes hit hard, especially against buildings, and they cost much less than Hand Cannoneers for similar results. They pair well with Paladins, chopping down the Halberdiers and Camel Riders sent against the Frankish cavalry. Their long attack delay makes them poor at kiting.
tiger-cavalry: Wei heavy cavalry that grows stronger as it kills, gaining hit points and attack with each of its first four kills. Speed, solid pierce armor and a bonus against archers make it an archer hunter, and after one kill it drops Crossbowmen and Elite Skirmishers in two hits. With no melee armor of its own it is only middling in melee, so Heavy Hei Guang Cavalry often fight beside it. The unit is based on the Hu bao qi, the Tiger and Leopard Cavalry.
traction-trebuchet: Shu, Wei and Wu have no Trebuchets or Bombard Cannons, so the Traction Trebuchet is their only long-range weapon against buildings. It fires without packing or unpacking, prefers units over buildings and can even kite slow units, though it has no splash and, unlike a regular Trebuchet, Monks can convert it from range. Each civilization handles it differently: the Shu version moves faster and gets every upgrade, and the Wei version is cheaper and the easiest long-range siege weapon to mass.
trade-cart: In long games, once gold mines and Relics run dry, Trade Carts become the main source of gold. Each cart travels to another player's Market and back, and the payout grows roughly with the square of the distance, so far apart Markets pay much better. That makes the trade route a long, exposed line the enemy will want to raid. East Asian Trade Carts are pulled by African water buffaloes, an animal that has never been domesticated.
trade-cog: A cargo ship that earns gold by sailing between one of your Docks and another player's, and longer routes pay more per trip. It does on water what Trade Carts do on land, and since gold mines run out in long games, a protected sea route can keep an economy going. It has no attack, so enemy warships see it as an easy target. With Caravan and Dry Dock, the Berber Trade Cog is the fastest unit in the game.
transport-ship: Transport Ships carry land units across water. On island maps they are the only way to move an army, and elsewhere they open up overseas raids, sneak attacks and escapes from a lost fight, or act as decoys carrying one cheap unit to pull the enemy away. Everything on board sinks with the ship, so Galleys or Fire Ships should escort it. Converting a loaded enemy Transport traps the units inside, still taking up their owner's population.
trebuchet: The Trebuchet is the safest way to bring down a Castle, with the longest base range and highest attack of any unit. It must unpack before firing and pack before moving, both slow, and it is inaccurate against units, so it needs an army around it, and players use Attack Ground so targets cannot dodge. It is also the only unit that catches fire like a building when damaged, and players still joke about it firing a 90 kg payload over 300 meters.
turtle-ship: Korea's armored gunboat fires a cannonball and then two volleys of rockets in every attack cycle. Its armor cancels the anti-ship bonus most ships and towers rely on, so Galleons and Fire Ships take ages to sink one, and it has no minimum range. Slow and costly, it belongs in the middle of a fleet with faster ships around it. Admiral Yi Sun-shin won two great victories with the real Turtle Ships during the Japanese invasion of 1592.
two-handed-swordsman: A short stop on the Militia line between Long Swordsman and Champion, and the only upgrade in the game that adds attack without improving defense. Because the Champion upgrade opens up right away, it is rarely kept for long, though it still breaks Halberdier and ram pushes before a Champion is worth the price. The Malay can make it a trash unit with Forced Levy, which swaps its gold cost for food, and Bulgarian ones get extra melee armor and free upgrades.
urumi-swordsman: A Dravidian swordsman whose charged first strike deals heavy damage with a splash. A group crashing into packed archers can wipe them out in seconds, and Urumis guarding siege or Armored Elephants punish anything that runs around them. Once the charge is spent it is a fragile swordsman with no pierce armor, so its fights tend to go very well or very badly. A real urumi is a flexible steel band that can be coiled around the waist like a belt.
varangian-guard: The Varangian Guard is generalist heavy infantry for the Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Vikings, and it earns gold while fighting other units, which helps it trade well with most of the field. It is tougher, faster and quicker to upgrade fully than the Militia line, but it lacks their bonus against buildings and earns nothing from hitting them, so Champions stay better for razing. The real guard served the Byzantine emperor with recruits from Scandinavia, England and the Rus'.
villager: Every economy runs on Villagers: they gather all four resources, build, and repair buildings, ships and siege. Players keep making them for most of the game, often until they fill half the population or more. They are poor fighters, but garrisoned Villagers add arrows to Town Centers and towers, and a few behind an army can repair siege or build forward. Hunters, fishermen and builders are the same unit under a different title, and each new Villager's gender is picked at random.
war-chariot: A Shu chariot loaded with bolt throwers that switches between two modes: Focus Fire sends every bolt at one target and on through whatever stands behind it, while Barrage spreads more bolts over a wider area. Fast enough to stay away from infantry and tough against archers thanks to cavalry armor, it can wreck an unprepared economy early in the game. The design may come from the Wuhou Chariot, a mobile war machine with an automatic crossbow credited to Zhuge Liang.
war-elephant: The Persian War Elephant is individually stronger than any other unit and the most population-efficient in the game, which counts in a maxed out late game. It tramples whatever stands next to its target and flattens buildings that can barely scratch it. Even infantry can walk away from it, though, so it suits pitched battles, and Monks are a threat since the Persians lack Heresy. The game draws an African elephant, although the manual says the Persians got their elephants from India.
war-galley: The Galley line is the backbone of a navy, and the War Galley is where it starts to pull its weight. Its large bolts hit only the single target, with no pass-through, yet in numbers War Galleys handle Cannon Galleons, Demolition Ships and Transport Ships well and bombard units and buildings on the shore. Fire Ships are its natural enemy, so fleets usually mix the two. In any water fight, getting the War Galley upgrade quickly is treated as a must.
war-wagon: Korean armored carts that play like a much tougher, faster Arbalester. They can sit behind a melee line as ranged support or stand in front as a meat shield that shoots back, and they shrug off enough arrow fire to hit Villagers from inside Town Center range. Their large size makes them clumsy at hit and run and an easy target for Onagers. The unit was inspired by the Korean hwacha, though the real hwacha stood still and was used mostly in defense.
warrior-priest: An Armenian priest who fights like a Two-Handed Swordsman and also heals and picks up Relics like a Monk, though he cannot convert. That makes him a better Relic collector than a Monk: faster, quicker to train, and able to kill the enemy Monks going after the same Relics. Kept back on a passive stance, a few of them heal the army without being easily sniped. Fully upgraded, he has more hit points than any other foot soldier in the game.
white-feather-guard: A cheap, durable Shu polearm fighter whose job is standing in front of Shu archers and War Chariots. Every hit it lands slows the enemy, so cavalry diving at the backline gets caught and held off. Its own damage is low because the Shu lack the last Blacksmith attack upgrades, and with Liu Bei nearby it slowly heals. The historical White Feather Soldiers were an elite Shu Han force that mainly served as Liu Bei's personal guard.
winged-hussar: The Lithuanians and Poles get the Winged Hussar in place of the Hussar. It is a food-only trash unit that does the Hussar's job a little better, raiding and sniping Monks and siege, and it adds a bonus against gunpowder units that no other unit of the scout line has. That bonus nods to the Polish-Lithuanian hussars who charged the Ottoman gunpowder army at the Battle of Vienna, part of the largest cavalry charge in history. Neither civilization can fully upgrade it.
woad-raider: Celtic infantry that run faster than almost any other foot soldier, which fixes the usual infantry problem of never catching anything. That speed makes them raiders and siege hunters, good for running down a Trebuchet that is shelling your base, and they win most fights against ordinary infantry. The unit is an anachronism: the Picts painted themselves with woad about a thousand years before the medieval period, and the manual's claim that William Wallace was a woad raider comes from Braveheart.
xianbei-raider: The Wei replacement for the Cavalry Archer, weaker and frailer but light on gold, so it stays affordable late in the game. Every so often it fires a charged volley of extra arrows, enough to snipe Monks or punish Spearmen. With Ming Guang Armor it ends up with more melee armor than any other archer in the game. The unit is named after the Xianbei, a proto-Mongolic steppe people seen as ancestors of the Khitans and Mongols.
xolotl-warrior: A Knight in all but looks, with the jaguar skin and macuahuitl of the Jaguar Warrior, that the American civilizations can train only from a Stable they did not build themselves. Most get it by converting an enemy Stable after Redemption, which the Maya and Mapuche lack. Without Cavalier, Bloodlines or cavalry armor upgrades it falls behind as the game goes on, though it starts stronger in Post-Imperial games. Xolotl is the Aztec god of dogs, death and deformities.
